question: The CFO of a manufacturing company supports moving to Google Cloud but is uncomfortable that a variable monthly bill replaces the predictable, depreciated capital spend she is used to. She asks how the company can get cloud benefits while keeping a large share of spending predictable. What should you recommend?
options: Provision all resources at peak capacity from day one so that the bill never changes.
Purchase committed use discounts for the stable baseline of compute and database usage, keep elastic usage on demand, and set budgets with alerts so that variance is visible and controlled.
Prepay the estimated annual cloud spend to Google in January so that it can be capitalized like hardware.
Use only Spot VMs, whose lower price makes the monthly bill less significant.
explanation: The cloud model shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx, and predictability is achieved by committing to the baseline (committed use discounts provide a fixed, discounted charge for known steady-state usage) while paying on demand only for the elastic portion, with budgets and alerts giving finance visibility. Option A removes elasticity and overspends, defeating the purpose of the migration. Option C is not how Google Cloud billing works and prepayment does not by itself make the spending predictable or optimized. Option D uses preemptible capacity for workloads that may not tolerate it and does not make spending predictable.
hint: Core Rule (CapEx vs OpEx): The cloud model shifts spending from CapEx to OpEx, and predictability is achieved by committing to the baseline (committed use discounts provide a fixed, discounted charge for known steady-state usage) while paying on demand only for the elastic portion, with budgets and alerts giving finance visibility.

question: A visual effects studio renders frames overnight on Compute Engine. Each frame job takes about 10 minutes, is idempotent and can be restarted safely, and there is no hard deadline as long as the batch finishes by morning. Compute is 70% of the studio's cloud bill. How can the studio reduce compute cost the most without redesigning the workload?

Move the render jobs to GKE Autopilot to benefit from per-pod billing.
Reduce the machine size of each render VM so jobs take longer but cost less per hour.
Run the render workers as Spot VMs in a managed instance group with a job queue that requeues work when an instance is preempted.
explanation: Fault-tolerant, restartable batch work with flexible timing is the ideal profile for Spot VMs, which offer the largest Compute Engine discount in exchange for the possibility of preemption; a managed instance group and a queue handle recreation and requeueing so preemptions do not lose work. Option A locks in spend for a nightly workload that is idle most of the day and delivers a smaller discount than Spot pricing. Option B changes the platform without a clear cost advantage for GPU-heavy or CPU-heavy render jobs. Option C reduces hourly cost but not total cost, because the same amount of compute work still has to be done.
hint: Core Rule: Fault-tolerant, restartable batch work with flexible timing is the ideal profile for Spot VMs, which offer the largest Compute Engine discount in exchange for the possibility of preemption; a managed instance group and a queue handle recreation and requeueing so preemptions do not lose work.

question: A university provides Google Cloud sandbox projects to students for coursework. Each project has a monthly budget of $50 with email alerts, yet several students have accidentally left GPU VMs running and generated bills of hundreds of dollars before anyone read the email. The IT director wants spending in these sandbox projects to stop automatically at the budget limit, accepting that running workloads will be interrupted. What should you do?
options: Lower the budget alert thresholds to 25%, 50% and 75% so that students receive more warnings.
Configure the budget to automatically block resource creation once the limit is reached.

Connect the budget to a Pub/Sub topic and deploy a Cloud Run function that, when the notification shows cost exceeding the budget, removes the billing account from the project, and pair it with reduced GPU quotas on sandbox projects.
explanation: Cloud Billing budgets only notify; they never stop spending by themselves, so enforcing a hard cap requires a programmatic budget action: budget notifications published to Pub/Sub trigger a Cloud Run function that disables billing on the project, which stops all billable services. Lowering quotas on GPUs adds a preventive control. Option A produces more emails that students have already shown they do not act on. Option B describes a capability that budgets do not have. Option C relies on manual human action, which is exactly what failed.
hint: Core Rule (Budgets and programmatic actions): Cloud Billing budgets only notify; they never stop spending by themselves, so enforcing a hard cap requires a programmatic budget action: budget notifications published to Pub/Sub trigger a Cloud Run function that disables billing on the project, which stops all billable services.

question: A market research firm uses BigQuery on-demand pricing. Last month a single analyst ran an unfiltered query across a multi-petabyte table repeatedly from a dashboard, generating a five-figure charge in one day. question: A payments company must retain transaction audit logs for seven years. topic: Sustained use and committed use discounts
question: A ticketing company runs a fleet of N2 VMs in a managed instance group. About 40 instances run continuously, and the group scales to as many as 200 instances for a few days each month around major on-sale events. The FinOps team wants to maximize discounts on this fleet with minimal ongoing effort. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)
options: Purchase resource-based committed use discounts covering the 40 always-on instances' vCPUs and memory.
Purchase resource-based committed use discounts covering the full 200-instance peak.
Take no action for the burst instances: sustained use discounts are applied automatically to eligible N2 VMs based on how long they run within the month.
Switch the burst instances to E2 machine types so that they qualify for sustained use discounts.
Enable sustained use discounts in the Cloud Billing console for the project.
explanation: The correct pattern is to commit only to the baseline and let automatic discounts handle the variable portion: committed use discounts on the 40 steady instances give the deepest discount without stranding, and sustained use discounts apply automatically to eligible machine families such as N2 in proportion to monthly runtime, with nothing to configure. Option B would leave most of the commitment unused and billed during the majority of the month. Option D is wrong because E2 machine types are not eligible for sustained use discounts. Option E is wrong because sustained use discounts cannot be enabled or disabled; they are applied automatically.

question: An ad-tech company stores clickstream data in a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1 and runs its nightly Dataflow and Dataproc processing jobs in europe-west1 because that is where the team originally set up its projects. The jobs read tens of terabytes each night. Billing analysis shows large network charges attributed to these jobs. Which change most directly reduces this cost?
options: Compress the clickstream files so that less data is transferred between regions.
Run the processing jobs in us-central1, the same region as the bucket, so that reads are within-region and do not incur inter-region data transfer charges.
Enable Cloud CDN in front of the Cloud Storage bucket to cache the files for the jobs.
Move the bucket to a multi-region location so that reads from Europe are free.
explanation: Reading Cloud Storage data from compute in a different region incurs inter-region data transfer charges on every read, so colocating processing with data eliminates the charge entirely and also improves throughput. Option A reduces the volume but still pays cross-region rates on every byte and adds CPU cost. Option C is designed for cacheable public content delivered to users, not for bulk analytical reads. Option D is wrong because reading a multi-region bucket from a region incurs data transfer charges too and increases storage cost.
hint: Core Rule (Data locality and network cost): Reading Cloud Storage data from compute in a different region incurs inter-region data transfer charges on every read, so colocating processing with data eliminates the charge entirely and also improves throughput.

question: A machine learning startup wants to cut its Compute Engine bill by moving as much as possible to Spot VMs. The architect must decide which workloads are appropriate. Which two workloads are good candidates for Spot VMs? (Choose two.)
options: The self-managed PostgreSQL primary instance that backs the customer-facing API.
Stateless CI build agents that pick up jobs from a queue and can be retried on failure.
The stateful game-session servers that hold in-memory player state for the duration of a match.
Model training jobs that checkpoint to Cloud Storage every few minutes and can resume from the last checkpoint.
The single VM that hosts the company's on-call paging integration.
explanation: Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with short notice and have no availability guarantee, so they suit workloads that are fault tolerant and can resume or be retried: queue-driven CI agents and checkpointed training jobs lose little work on preemption and benefit from the deep discount. Option A is a stateful primary database whose preemption would cause an outage and possible data loss. Option C holds unreplicated in-memory state that would be lost mid-match. Option E is a critical single point of failure for incident response and must not run on preemptible capacity.
hint: Core Rule (Spot VM suitability): Spot VMs can be preempted at any time with short notice and have no availability guarantee, so they suit workloads that are fault tolerant and can resume or be retried: queue-driven CI agents and checkpointed training jobs lose little work on preemption and benefit from the deep discount.

question: A software vendor runs 120 development and test VMs on Compute Engine that are used only during business hours on weekdays, yet they run 24/7. The engineering manager wants to cut the cost of these environments with minimal effort and without changing how developers work during the day. What should you do?
options: Purchase one-year committed use discounts for the development VMs.
Ask developers to stop their VMs at the end of each day.
Attach an instance schedule (resource policy) to the development VMs that stops them every evening and on weekends and starts them each weekday morning.
Convert the development VMs to Spot VMs.
